If Lancashire thus consists of parts historically unconnected, there is also much variety in the topography of the different parts.
The Lancashire place-names consequently offer many interesting and difficult problems.

In O.W. and O.Bret, it was a loose m or nasalised v, and in Breton the preceding vowel is still nasalised (Pedersen L, p. 161ff.). That in Welsh a loose m or nasalised v was spoken comparatively late is proved by such spellings as O.W. amal (Pedersen I.e.) or Tarn for Taf, etc., in LL.

But the name Hanging Chadder in Thornham cannot be so explained, and it is reasonable to identify the first el. of Chadderton with that name. Chadder may be a Brit, name identical with Welsh coder " a hill fort " (=Ir. cathir), from earlier *cater (cognate with L. caterva).

The township occupies the S. slope of a hill, which was no doubt originally called Rainhill. Lindkvist p. 72 suggests as first el. O.N. rein " strip of land forming the boundary of a field or estate," and points out that the hill forms the boundary against Eccleston.
But it is doubtful if rein could be used of such a boundary ; the fields of Eccleston and RainhiU hardly met on the hill.

It seems plausible that Rainhill and Rainford have the same first el. The earfy forms of the latter point to a dissyllabic first oheme (Raine-) ; in Rainhill thfe unstressed vowel would be dropped early before the h-, which was often silent.
